source.title: Who Pays and How Much
source.summary: Tax incidence, deadweight loss, and how Islamic tax instruments compare to modern systems.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Taxes change behavior. Income taxes discourage earning; sales taxes discourage spending; property taxes discourage holding. The economics of tax design is about minimizing these distortions while raising enough revenue. This episode covers tax incidence (who really bears the burden), deadweight loss, and the efficiency-equity tradeoff. Then it examines Islamic tax instruments: zakat as a wealth tax with a 2.5% rate and nisab threshold, kharaj as a land/output tax, ushur as a trade levy. Each has specific economic properties. Zakat's flat rate is simple but possibly insufficient for a modern state. The jizya receives an honest treatment: discriminatory by modern standards, though it had a specific fiscal logic in its historical context.

linkedin.post: Tax design is fundamentally about behavior modification. Income taxes discourage earning, sales taxes discourage spending, property taxes discourage holding assets. Every tax creates deadweight loss through behavioral distortions. Islamic tax instruments approached this differently. Zakat's 2.5% wealth tax discourages hoarding without penalizing productive investment or consumption. Kharaj targeted land productivity. Ushur applied to trade flows. Each had specific economic properties designed for particular outcomes. The challenge remains efficiency versus equity. Zakat's flat rate keeps administration simple but may be insufficient for modern state revenue needs. The question isn't whether these systems are perfect, but what their economic logic can teach us about tax incidence and deadweight loss. short_video.title: Why Zakat Creates Different Economic Incentives
short_video.hook: Every tax changes behavior, but zakat does something different
short_video.voiceover: Income taxes make people work less. Sales taxes make people spend less. Property taxes make people hold fewer assets. Every tax creates what economists call deadweight loss through behavioral changes. But zakat's 2.5% wealth tax has a different property. It discourages hoarding money without penalizing productive investment or consumption. While modern tax systems often create conflicts between earning and spending, zakat creates incentives for capital deployment rather than accumulation. The question isn't whether 2.5% is the right rate for today, but whether the mechanism itself offers lessons for tax design.
